steps.title: Arousal
steps.body: A state of physical and psychological readiness and activation. It is the level of excitement, alertness and energy a performer experiences. Arousal exists on a continuum from deep sleep (very low) to extreme excitement or panic (very high).

steps.title: Inverted-U Theory (Yerkes-Dodson Law)
steps.body: The theory that performance improves as arousal increases, but only up to an optimal point. Beyond this point, further increases in arousal lead to a decline in performance. When graphed, this relationship forms an inverted U shape.

steps.title: Zone of Optimal Functioning (ZOF)
steps.body: Each individual performer has their own personal zone of optimal arousal where they perform at their best. This zone varies from person to person - some performers need high arousal to perform well, while others perform better at lower arousal levels.

steps.title: PE Exam Tips — Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory
steps.body: 1. For Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory questions, use subject-specific terminology precisely 2. Support every point with specific evidence or examples 3. Show balanced analysis — consider different perspectives before reaching a conclusion 4. Link your understanding of Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory to real-world contexts where possible 5. For longer answers, plan your response to address all parts of the question

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Define arousal and explain how it affects sporting performance using the inverted-U theory. | Explain why a rugby player needs a higher optimal arousal level than a snooker player. | Describe three stress management techniques a performer can use to reduce over-arousal.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always draw or describe the inverted-U shape when explaining the theory Link optimal arousal to skill type: gross/complex = high, fine/closed = low Know the three stress management techniques: deep breathing, visualisation, positive self-talk Explain HOW each technique works, not just what it is Use the term "zone of optimal functioning" to show understanding of individual differences Remember arousal can be too low (lethargic) as well as too high (anxious) - both need management
